title: Blues and Pentatonics
goal: Solo over a twelve-bar blues in A, knowing where the changes are and landing on notes that belong to them.
assumes: You can fret and pick single notes, and you can play eighth notes with a click at 70 BPM. You play no chords here: you hear them change under your lines. If A7, D7 and E7 are only names to you, First Chords and Strumming has a Step, 'Seventh chords and a twelve-bar blues in A', that strums this same blues. The shuffle is explained in Step 1, and Rhythm Foundations has a Step, 'Three to a beat', on triplets and the shuffle if you want more of it. Nothing about scales or blues is assumed. New ideas arrive in A, on purpose, so that theory is the only new thing, and the Steps after them move to other keys. This is a long Path: about three months at fifteen to twenty minutes a day.

skills: Eighth notes with a click at 70 BPM

orderRationale: Theory arrives as written lines you can be graded on, and choosing your own notes comes after, as a short 'your turn' at the end of a Step. Chord tones arrive early, as soon as the box is in the hand, as arpeggios of A7, D7 and E7 in box 1, each followed by a lick that ends on the chord's third, before the blue notes: knowing where the chord is matters more than knowing an extra note. Call and response follows because written answers to one call teach phrase length and endings with almost no theory. The blues scale and bends come after the player can find the chord tones, so neither becomes a thing to sit on. A second box comes late on purpose: more notes before good choices makes for faster bad solos. Guide tones come near the end because they are the most abstract idea here and easiest once the form is in the ear. Slow blues comes last as it hides nothing. Between the ideas sit Steps that add little or nothing new: the box in other keys, the same notes over a straight band, the thirds in new keys, the quick change, the minor blues, two more boxes, and sixths. The blues is a style a player stays in for months, and each of those Steps takes what was just learned somewhere new before the next idea arrives. A second round of such Steps sits the same way. Two finished pieces are also taken to a second key straight after they are learned: the minor blues moves to D minor near the end of the Intermediate Level, and the three-chorus solo is built again in E, from the nut to the twelfth fret. In the Intermediate Level the form in E at the nut, with its turnarounds, follows bends: by then the twelve bars, the walking line and the riffs are known, so a new key arrives on lines the player already has. Question and answer phrases close that Level, after the minor blues, because the Step ends on a chorus of the player's own that gathers what the Level taught. In the Advanced Level box 5 follows boxes 3 and 4 and completes the five shapes; the three-chorus solo sits straight after it, in A and then in E, because what it puts in order is the boxes, the slides between them and a bend at the top, so it closes the work on the neck; major and minor together, sixths and guide tones follow as the work on harmony, and the slow blues closes that; and the slow blues in C comes last, as the hardest Step taken to a second key.
gradingLimits: Graded Exercises are written lines: the app checks timing evenness, notes heard and extra notes, and right notes after the take where the notes are single, far enough apart and not ringing into each other; elsewhere right notes read 'not checked'. Timing over the shuffle band is judged against the written triplet with a looser bar, so a lighter or heavier swing is not marked down, and a constant lean behind the beat costs nothing at all. The right-note check has only been tried on computer-made guitar sound with no band in the mix, so direct input or headphones are the honest way to play anything with a band; with a microphone and speakers it is untested. A bent note would read as a wrong one, so bends are timed and never pitch-checked: the unison bends are double stops, which the note check leaves alone. Landing on chord tones, staying in the scale, keeping rests and choosing your own notes are not measured today: those Exercises are 'your turn', self-checked and labelled 'not checked yet'. Nothing here grades feel.

steps.title: Pentatonic box 1
steps.goal: Play the A minor pentatonic box over a shuffle band, find its three A's inside a riff, and play your first twelve bars.
steps.why: These five notes are most of the blues and rock you've ever heard. Learning one box well, and knowing which of its notes is home, gets you playing over a band today. Without that home note, the box is a pattern: with it, it's a map you can navigate. Everything here is played with the band from the first note, because the box only makes sense against a groove.
howTo: First finger stays on fret 5, one finger per fret. The notes are A, C, D, E, G, and every string uses two of them.
The root is the note a chord is named after.

Here the root is A, and the three A's are home: fret 5 on the low E, fret 7 on the D string, fret 5 on the high E. Every Exercise in this Step starts or lands on one of them, so say 'A' when you get there.
The band is a drummer and a bassist in place of the click.
If you get lost, stop, find beat 1 of the next bar and come back in there.

Shuffle eighths are long-short. Each beat is split into three even parts, a triplet: count '1-trip-let, 2-trip-let' and play on the number and the 'let'. Damp strings you aren't using with the side of your picking hand.
steps.payoff: You can play a whole twelve-bar chorus over a shuffle band, and you always know where home is.

exercises.title: Box 1 over the shuffle
exercises.purpose: Put the shape in the hand with the band behind you: up the box, the top A held, back down, and home on the low A. Four bars that loop, so the scale turns into a groove.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.

Bar 1 climbs from the low A at fret 5 to D on the G string. Bar 2: E, G, A, C on the top two strings, then hold the high A for two beats. Bar 3 comes down to the A on the D string, a quarter note on beat 3, then G. Bar 4: E, D, C and the low A, held.
First finger on fret 5, third finger on fret 7, fourth on fret 8. Say the A's out loud as you pass them.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and the shuffle are what this asks. Tempo isn't the point yet.

cues.say: Say each A out loud as you pass it.
Use finger one for each note at fret five.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count each held A's two beats, then move on.
Land each new string right on its beat.
Hold the low A its full two beats.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Find the three A's
exercises.purpose: The root is home, and every phrase you make will be judged by your ear against it. Here one little riff starts from each A in turn, low, middle and high, so you find them without looking, in time, with the band.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Four bars that loop.

Bar 1 from the low A (low E string, fret 5): A, C, D, C, A, C, D, E. Bar 2 from the middle A (D string, fret 7): A, C, D, C, A, G, E, G. Bar 3 from the high A (high E, fret 5): A, C, A, G, E, G, A, G. Bar 4: E, D, C, D, and the middle A held for two beats.
Every bar starts on an A. Listen to the same note in three octaves, and to how the riff sounds darker low and brighter high.
exercises.coachLine: Every bar starts on an A. I check the notes and the shuffle after the take.

cues.say: Start each riff on its A without looking.
Find the low, middle and high A first.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each bar's first note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count the held A's two beats, then the low A.
Hold the hand still as the pick changes strings.
Hold the last A for its full two beats.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Your first lick over A7
exercises.purpose: A written two-bar lick over the shuffle band: down the box from the top A, then home to the A on the D string. The first time the box sounds like a record.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, long-short on the band's triplet, 55 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Bar 1: A, C, A, G, E, D, C, D, from the high E string down to the G string. Bar 2: A on the D string, C, G, and the A again, held for two beats.
Swing it the way the drummer does. If the long-short feels odd, count '1-trip-let' and play on the '1' and the 'let'.
exercises.coachLine: Written notes, so I can check them after the take, and the timing against a shuffle that allows for your own swing.

cues.say: Play long-short, like the drummer's shuffle.
Name the notes as you play: A, C, A, G.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count the last A's two beats, then start again.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Keep the long-short swing right to the last A.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Your first twelve bars
exercises.purpose: A whole chorus of the blues in box 1, built the way real players build one: the lick, then the A riff, said again over D7, then a new line over E7 and D7 that comes home. Twelve bars of playing, with the chords changing under you.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. A blues is a form of twelve bars that goes round and round, and one time round is a chorus. The chords are A7 for four bars, D7 for two, A7 for two, then E7, D7, A7 and E7. You don't play them: you hear them change under your line.
Bars 1 and 2 are your first lick, and bars 3 and 4 the low and middle A riffs. Bars 5 to 8 are the same four bars again: the lick sounds different over D7 because the chord has moved, not the notes.
Bar 9 starts on E for the E7, bar 10 on D for the D7, bar 11 lands on the middle A, and bar 12 holds E over the E7, which pulls you back to the top.

Shake the last E if you like: push the string a little and let it back, over and over. That shake is called vibrato. It isn't graded: the app checks that E was the note and on time, and the shake is yours.
exercises.coachLine: Twelve written bars over the band: I check the notes and the shuffle after the take. The vibrato on the last E isn't graded.

cues.say: Count the twelve bars as they go by.
Play the same line over D7 as over A7.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count the held note's two beats, then go on.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Hold the last E for two beats, then stop.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: The box in other keys
steps.goal: Move box 1 to G, C and E and play the lines you already know there, then a whole chorus in a key that changes.
steps.why: The box is a shape, and a shape can start on any fret. The note under your first finger on the low E string names the key: fret 3 is G, fret 5 is A, fret 8 is C, fret 12 is E. Songs are not all in A, and the first time a band calls a blues in G you want your hand to go to fret 3 without thinking. Nothing here is new to the fingers. What is new is finding home somewhere else.
howTo: Find the root on the low E string with your first finger, and the box is under your hand: the same frets as before, counted from there.

Before you play, find the three roots in the new place, as you found the three A's. They are in the same spots in the shape: low E string under the first finger, D string under the third, high E under the first.
Low on the neck the frets are wider and high up they are narrower. Give yourself a slower tempo for the first take in each new place.
steps.payoff: The box is no longer a place at the fifth fret. It goes where the key goes.

exercises.title: The box in G
exercises.purpose: The four-bar box loop from Step 1, two frets lower, over a band in G. Same fingers, same order, a new home.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. First finger on fret 3, third finger on fret 5, fourth on fret 6.

Bar 1 climbs from the low G at fret 3 to C on the G string. Bar 2 goes over the top two strings and holds the high G for two beats. Bar 3 comes down to the G on the D string, fret 5, on beat 3, then F. Bar 4 ends on the low G, held.
Say 'G' on each of the three G's as you pass them.
exercises.coachLine: The same line as Step 1, two frets down. I check the notes and the shuffle after the take.

cues.say: Say 'G' as you pass each of the three G's.
Use finger one for each note at fret three.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count each held G's two beats, then move on.
Land each new string right on its beat.
Hold the low G its full two beats.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Three C's in the box at the eighth fret
exercises.purpose: The riff that starts from each root in turn, moved up to C. Low, middle and high C, each opening a bar.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. First finger on fret 8.

Bar 1 starts on the low C (low E string, fret 8). Bar 2 starts on the middle C (D string, fret 10). Bar 3 starts on the high C (high E string, fret 8). Bar 4 comes down and holds the middle C for two beats.
The frets are closer together here than at the fifth fret. Keep one finger per fret and let the hand feel smaller.
exercises.coachLine: The first three bars each start on a C, and the last one lands on a C. I check the notes and the shuffle after the take.

cues.say: Start each riff on its C without looking.
Keep one finger per fret from fret eight.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each bar's first note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count the held C's two beats, then the low C.
Hold the hand still as the pick changes strings.
Hold the last C for its full two beats.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Your first lick, at the twelfth fret
exercises.purpose: The two-bar lick from Step 1 in E, up at the twelfth fret where the double dots are. E is the key guitar players call most often.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 55 BPM up to a pass at 90. First finger on fret 12, third finger on fret 14, fourth on fret 15.
Bar 1 comes down from the high E at fret 12 on the top string to the G string. Bar 2 lands on the E on the D string, fret 14, and holds it at the end for two beats.
If the body of the guitar is in the way up here, bring your thumb round toward the bottom of the neck.
exercises.coachLine: The same lick, seven frets up. Notes and the shuffle after the take.

cues.say: Start the lick on the top string, fret twelve.
Keep the first finger on fret twelve.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count the last E's two beats, then start again.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Keep the shuffle going right to the last E.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Twelve bars in a new key
exercises.purpose: Your first chorus from Step 1, all twelve bars, in G, C or D. The chords are in the new key and the same line follows them.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Look at which key came up, put your first finger on its root on the low E string, and play the chorus you know from there: fret 3 for G, fret 8 for C, fret 10 for D.
The form has not changed: four bars on the first chord, two on the second, two back home, then one bar each of the third chord, the second, home, and the third again.
exercises.coachLine: Twelve written bars in a key that changes from day to day. Notes and the shuffle after the take.

cues.say: Find the key's root before you start.
Keep one finger per fret for the whole chorus.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count the held note's two beats, then go on.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Hold the last note for two beats, then stop.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: The same notes, a straight feel
steps.goal: Play box 1 in even eighths over a straight rock band, and a twelve-bar chorus of riffs that follow the chords.
steps.why: Half the blues you know is not a shuffle. Rock and roll, and most blues-rock, play the eighth notes even: one-and-two-and, both halves the same length. The notes are the same five and the form is the same twelve bars. Only the feel changes, and a player who has only shuffled will swing a straight groove without meaning to. Playing the same box both ways is how the hand learns the difference.
howTo: Even eighths: 'one-and-two-and', with the 'and' exactly halfway. No long-short. If it starts to lilt, you are shuffling.
Pick down on the beat and up on the 'and'. The riffs here stay on the low strings; rest the side of the picking hand lightly near the bridge so they stay tight.
Listen to the hi-hat. In a straight groove it plays the same even eighths you do.
steps.payoff: You can hear whether a band is shuffling or playing straight, and your eighths follow it.

exercises.title: Box 1, even eighths
exercises.purpose: The four-bar box loop you know, with the band playing straight. The notes are those of Step 1: the only thing to change is how long each eighth is.
howTo: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Up the box from the low A to D on the G string, over the top and hold the high A, down to the A on the D string, and home to the low A.
Every eighth the same length. Count 'one-and-two-and' out loud for the first take.
exercises.coachLine: Straight eighths now, so the timing bar is tighter than over the shuffle. Notes and evenness after the take.

cues.say: Make every eighth the same length.
Use finger one for each note at fret five.
Pick every eighth, the first and the second.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Land each beat's first eighth with the drums.
Wait for the drums on each beat's first eighth.
Count each held A's two beats, then move on.
Land each new string right on its beat.
Hold the low A its full two beats.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: A straight lick
exercises.purpose: A two-bar lick that runs down the box in even eighths and comes home to A. The kind of line a shuffle would smooth over; here every note is on its own.
howTo: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Bar 1: A on the top string, then G, E, D, C, and A on the D string, then C and D on the G string. Bar 2: A on the D string for a beat, then G and A, and the A held for two beats.
exercises.coachLine: Notes and even eighths after the take.

cues.say: Keep the eighths even as the lick runs down.
Go back up to the G string for C and D.
Pick every eighth, the first and the second.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Land each beat's first eighth with the drums.
Wait for the drums on each beat's first eighth.
Count each held A to its end, then go on.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Hold the last A for its full two beats.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: A riff on the low strings
exercises.purpose: One bar on the two lowest strings, built on the low A, that loops. Blues-rock rhythm guitar is made of riffs like this one.
howTo: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90. One bar, round and round.
A, A, C, A on the low E string (frets 5, 5, 8, 5), then D on the A string, the low A again, and E and D on the A string (frets 7 and 5).
Down-up all the way. The two A's at the start are a down and an up on the same note.
exercises.coachLine: One bar that loops. Notes and even eighths after the take.

cues.say: Pick down-up all the way through.
Play the C at fret eight on the low E string.
Pick both A's at the start of the riff.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Land each beat's first eighth with the drums.
Wait for the drums on each beat's first eighth.
Hold the hand still as the pick changes strings.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Twelve bars of riffs
exercises.purpose: A riff from each chord's root: from A for the A7 bars, from D for the D7 bars, from E for the E7 bar. A whole chorus of rhythm playing, all inside box 1.
howTo: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 85.

Over A7, the riff you just learned. Over D7 it starts on D (A string, fret 5): D, D, E, D, then G on the D string, D, and A and G on the D string. Over E7 it starts on E (A string, fret 7): E, E, G, E, A, E, G, E.
Bar 12 is the ending: E, G, A, G, and E held for two beats. Then the form comes round again.
Each riff starts on its chord's root. If you lose your place, listen for the bass: it is playing the same roots.
exercises.coachLine: Twelve bars over the band. I check the notes and the even eighths after the take.

cues.say: Start each riff on its chord's root.
Start the D7 riff on the A string, fret five.
Pick both repeated notes at each riff's start.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Land each beat's first eighth with the drums.
Wait for the drums on each beat's first eighth.
Count the last E's two beats, then start again.
Hold the hand still as the pick changes strings.
Hold the last E for two beats, then stop.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: Chord tones: A7, D7 and E7
steps.goal: Play the arpeggio of each chord of the blues in box 1, and a lick that ends on each chord's third.
steps.why: This is the single biggest step from playing scales to playing changes. A wrong-sounding note is mostly a note that stopped in the wrong place. An arpeggio is the chord one note at a time, so after playing it you know where the chord lives in the box, and a lick that ends on the third says the chord's name out loud.
howTo: A7 is A, C#, E, G. D7 is D, F#, A, C. E7 is E, G#, B, D. The sign # is read 'sharp' and means one fret higher: C# is one fret above C. Flat means one fret lower. The notes of a chord are named by counting letters up from its root: in A7, C# is the third, E is the fifth and G is the flat seven, a seventh lowered by one fret. The thirds are C#, F# and G#.
Box 1 has no C#, F# or G#: they sit a fret below or beside its notes. That is why the arpeggios move the hand a little, and why they sound so different from the box.
Aim for the last note first, then get there. Decide on it a beat early.
steps.payoff: The same box suddenly follows the chords, and you can hear the third land.

exercises.title: A on every downbeat
exercises.purpose: Written phrases that land on A at every bar line. The feel of arriving, before it becomes a choice.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 70 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Two beats of A on the D string, then four shuffle eighths that walk away and come back. Land on the next bar line as if it were the point of the whole bar, because it is.
exercises.coachLine: Written notes, and every one of them lands back on A. I check the notes and the shuffle.

cues.say: Land on the A right as each bar starts.
Play every held A at fret seven, D string.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put the held A right on '1' each time.
Wait for '1' before the held A.
Count the A's two beats, then walk away.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Lead the last four notes back to the A.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: The A7 arpeggio, and a lick to C#
exercises.purpose: A7 one note at a time from the low root, then a lick that comes down the box and moves up one fret from C to C#, the chord's own third.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, then a half note, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80.

Bar 1, up: A at fret 5 on the low E (second finger), C# at fret 4 on the A string (first finger), E at 7, G at 5 and A at 7 on the D string, C# at 6 on the G string, E at 5 and G at 8 on the B string. Let the hand move up a fret after the C# on the G string, so the fourth finger reaches fret 8 without a stretch.
Bar 2: G, E, D, C, then C# at fret 6 on the G string for two beats. That move of one fret, a half step, from C to C# is the sound of the blues coming to rest.
exercises.coachLine: A written arpeggio and lick: I check each note and the timing after the take.

cues.say: Move from C up to C# and hold it.
Second finger on the low A, first on the C#.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count the C#'s two beats, then the low A.
Move up a fret after the C# on the G string.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Walk down G, E, D, C, then settle on C#.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: The D7 arpeggio, and a lick to F#
exercises.purpose: D7 from its root on the A string, then a lick that steps down from G to F#, D7's third. Over the D7, that one note is what makes the change audible.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, then a half note, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80.

Bar 1, up: D at fret 5 on the A string, F# at 4 and A at 7 on the D string, C at 5 and D at 7 on the G string, F# at 7 on the B string, A at 5 and C at 8 on the high E. First finger starts on fret 4 for the F#, and the hand moves up a fret for the top two strings.
Bar 2: A, C, A on the high E, G at fret 8 on the B string, then down a fret to F# and hold it.
exercises.coachLine: Written notes again, checked after the take, with the timing against the shuffle.

cues.say: Step down from G to F# and hold it.
Put the first finger on fret four for the F#.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count the F#'s two beats, then the D.
Move up a fret for the top two strings.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Walk down A, C, A, G, then settle on F#.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: The E7 arpeggio, and a lick to G#
exercises.purpose: E7 from its root at fret 7 on the A string, a step up the neck, then a lick that ends on G#, the third that pulls the form back home to A.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, then a half note, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80.

Bar 1, up: E at fret 7 on the A string, G# at 6 and B at 9 on the D string, D at 7 and E at 9 on the G string, G# at 9 on the B string, B at 7 and D at 10 on the high E. First finger on fret 6, then up a fret for the top two strings.
Bar 2: B, D, B on the high E, A at 10 on the B string, then down a fret to G# and hold it. It's the D7 lick moved up two frets.

steps.title: Call and response
steps.goal: Hear a phrase, answer it, and leave space: the conversation that blues is built on.
steps.why: Blues is a conversation, and most beginners only ever talk. Answering a phrase teaches you to phrase in lengths a listener can follow, and it forces you to stop playing. It does more for how you sound, per minute, than any scale you can learn.
howTo: Listen to the whole call before you play. Don't start your answer until it has finished.
Keep your answer about as long as the call. Two bars of question deserves two bars of answer.
Silence is a note. A bar with nothing in it is a decision, and a good one.
steps.payoff: You can trade two-bar phrases with the app and it sounds like a conversation.

exercises.title: Echo
exercises.purpose: The app plays a two-bar phrase; you play it back, note for note. Exercising the ear is what this is for.
howTo: Straight eighths and quarters, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80. Bars 1 and 2 are the call, bars 3 and 4 are yours.
Try not to look at the tab. Sing the phrase back before you play it, once, if you can.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I can say if the echo had the right notes and steady time. It's fine to take a few tries.

cues.say: Sing the call back before you play it.
Start the echo on the call's first note.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Stay silent while the call plays.
Come in on '1' right after the call ends.
Wait for '1' after the call before you start.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Play the last A short and stop.

exercises.feedbackNote: The app has to play the call: the synth voice can do that, and the Exercise format carries it as a guide part, but nothing wires that up yet, so the call is in the tab for now.

exercises.title: One call, four answers

Answer 1 ends on A (finished). Answer 2 ends on E (open). Answer 3 ends on G (it wants to go on). Answer 4 climbs to the high C (it hangs in the air).
Let each last note ring through its two beats, then stop.
exercises.coachLine: Four written answers: I check the notes and the time after the take. Which ending you like best is yours.

steps.title: Landing on the third, in new keys
steps.goal: Play the arpeggio and its lick to the third in G and C, then a twelve-bar chorus whose phrases stop on each chord's third.
steps.why: You have met the two ideas that matter most at this Level: the box moves with the key, and a phrase sounds right when it stops on a note of the chord. This Step puts them together before anything new arrives. The third is the note that says whether a chord is major, so a phrase that stops on it tells the listener which chord is under it, with no band needed.
howTo: The third of the home chord sits one fret above the minor pentatonic's own third: in A, C# is one fret above C. In every key it is the same move, one fret up on the same string.

The thirds in A: C# over A7 (G string, fret 6), F# over D7 (D string, fret 4), G# over E7 (D string, fret 6). The F# is a fret below the box, so the first finger reaches back for it. So is the B over E7 (G string, fret 4).
Hold each landing note for its full two beats. The rest of the phrase is the way there.
steps.payoff: A chorus with no band would still tell a listener where the changes are.

steps.title: The blues scale and the blue notes
steps.goal: Add the flat five as a note to pass through, and hear the third move from C to C#.
steps.why: Two notes turn a scale into the blues. The flat five, Eb in A, sounds wrong on its own and wonderful on its way somewhere else. The blue third, C rubbing against the chord's C#, is the tension the whole style runs on. You've been playing the C already; now you'll hear what it's doing.
howTo: The A blues scale is A, C, D, Eb, E, G. Eb is E flat, one fret below E: fret 6 on the A string and fret 8 on the G string in this box.
Don't park on the Eb. Walk through it on your way to D or E.
A hammer-on is a note the fretting hand sounds alone: pick the lower note, then bring a finger down hard and fast on the higher fret of the same string.
To resolve the blue third, hammer from C to C# with your first and second fingers on the G string.
steps.payoff: One extra note, and suddenly the lick sounds like the blues rather than a rock scale.

exercises.title: A blues scale, box 1

steps.title: Following the 12-bar
steps.goal: Know where you are in the form without counting bars, and hear the turnaround coming.
steps.why: Losing your place is the number one bedroom problem. The form is twelve bars: four of A7, two of D7, two of A7, then E7, D7, A7, E7. Once it's in your ear you stop counting and start anticipating, and that's when solos start to have a shape. Playing the bass line is the fastest way there: you can't get lost when you're the one playing it.
howTo: Count the form as 4 + 4 + 4, as the Jam timeline does. Each four is a sentence.
Listen for the bar 9 change to E7. It's the moment the form really moves.
Bars 11 and 12 are the turnaround: they exist only to bring you back to the top.
steps.payoff: You hear the changes coming, and you can play a whole written chorus that brings the form home.

Hold the last E through all four beats.

steps.title: The quick change
steps.goal: Follow the twelve-bar form when it goes to the D7 in bar 2, with roots, a boogie line and a written chorus.
steps.why: Many blues songs do not sit on the first chord for four bars. They go to the second chord in bar 2 and come straight back: the quick change. Nothing else in the form moves. A player who has learned the form by counting gets caught by it every time; a player who listens hears it coming. It is the same twelve bars with one bar different, which makes it a good test of whether you know the form or only its length.
howTo: The form: A7, D7, A7, A7, then D7, D7, A7, A7, then E7, D7, A7, E7. Only bar 2 is new.
Before you play, listen to the band once through and point at bar 2 when the chord moves.
Everything you play here uses notes and shapes you already know: the roots and the boogie line from the last Step, and the thirds from the Beginner Level. What changes is when.
steps.payoff: When a song goes to its second chord in bar 2, you are already there.

exercises.title: Roots through the quick change

howTo: Whole notes, one a bar, 70 BPM up to a pass at 90.
A at fret 5 on the low E, D at fret 5 and E at fret 7 on the A string. Bar 2 is D, and bar 3 is A again.
exercises.coachLine: Twelve notes, each the right root, each on the bar. Bar 2 is the one to listen for.

cues.say: Go to D for bar two, then straight back.
Play D and E on the A string, A on the low E.
Pick each root firmly and let it ring.

Have the next root's finger ready early.
Hold the last E through all four beats.

exercises.purpose: The walking line you know, with its shape moved to D for bar 2 and back for bar 3. The hand moves to D for one bar and straight back.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, all twelve bars, 70 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Root, third, fifth, sixth, flat seven and back down, on each bar's chord. On D it starts at fret 5 on the A string; on E at fret 7 on the A string.
Look at the next root during the last two notes of each bar.
exercises.coachLine: A lot of notes and a form with a surprise in bar 2. Notes and time after the take.

Start the D bar at fret five on the A string.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.

Keep the pick small as you cross.
Keep the walk going right to the last note.

exercises.title: A written chorus on the quick change
exercises.purpose: Twelve bars of phrases that say the changes: F# over the D7 in bar 2, C# once the A7 is back, G# over the E7.
howTo: Shuffle eighths and half notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80.

Bar 1 is a phrase around E on the B string and the A above it, ending on the E. Bar 2, over D7, comes down to A and stops on F# (D string, fret 4). Bar 3 is bar 1 again, and bar 4 goes from C to C# and home to A.
Bars 5 and 6, over D7: a phrase around C, then F#, A, C, A and down to D. Bar 7 lands on C# and bar 8 holds A.
Bar 9, over E7, starts on B and ends on G# (D string, fret 6). Bar 10 ends on D. Bar 11 goes A, C, C#, E, G, E, and bar 12 holds E on the A string, fret 7.
exercises.coachLine: Twelve written bars. Notes and the shuffle after the take.

cues.say: Land on F# as the D7 arrives in bar two.
Reach fret four on the D string for F#.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count the held note's two beats, then go on.
Arrive at the new fret right on its beat.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.

steps.title: Bends that land
steps.goal: Bend a note up to an exact pitch, on time, and come back down from it.
steps.why: A bend is the guitar's voice, and it's only expressive when it arrives. A bend that stops short sounds like a mistake in a way a wrong note often doesn't. The way to learn it is simple, and it's old: play the note you want, then bend up to it and compare.
howTo: Bend with three fingers on the string, ring finger on the note. Push from the wrist, as if turning a door handle, rather than from the fingers alone.
Play the target first. Then bend until there's no wobble left between what you hear and what you remember.
The app times your bends and doesn't measure how far they go, so your ear judges the pitch on every one of these. Keep your strings fresh: old strings make this much harder.
Vibrato is a bend kept very small: push the string a little and let it back, over and over, at an even speed.
steps.payoff: A bent note that sits on the band's chord tone and arrives on the beat.

exercises.title: Target first, then bend
exercises.purpose: Play the note, then bend up to it from a whole step below, two frets: E, then D bent to E; A, then G bent to A; D, then C bent to D.
howTo: Half notes, 50 to 80 BPM: two beats on the target, two beats on the bend.
Hold the top of the bend without moving it. Use your ear and nothing else.
exercises.coachLine: I can't measure how far a bend goes, so your ear decides this one. Compare it to the note you just played.

cues.say: Play the target, then bend until it matches.

notes: A bend is one attack. The app can time it; it does not measure how far it travelled.

selfCheck: Does the top of the bend match the note you played just before, with no wobble between them?
Could you hold the top of the bend for the full two beats?

exercises.title: The half-step bend to C#
exercises.purpose: From C up to the chord's own third. It's a small, exact bend and it's the classic blues sound, moving from the blue third to the major third over A7.
howTo: Half notes over the shuffle, 60 to 90 BPM.
Fret 9 on the top string is your C#: play that first. Then fret 8 bent a half step. A half step feels like almost nothing, which is why it often overshoots.
exercises.coachLine: Half-step bends tend to go sharp, and it takes your ear to catch it.

cues.say: Bend fret eight until it sounds like fret nine.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
A bend is one attack. The app can time it; it does not measure how far it travelled.

selfCheck: Did the bend reach the C# you played first, and stop there rather than going past it?

exercises.title: Bends on the beat
exercises.purpose: A bend needs to arrive on time too, and that part the app can help with: it times when each bend was picked and whether it was heard.
howTo: Quarter notes, one bend on each beat of the first bar, 60 BPM up to a pass at 75.
G string fret 7 bent to E, B string fret 8 bent to A, twice, then the last bend held with vibrato. Start the bend as you pick and reach the top quickly. Your ear still decides if it landed.
exercises.coachLine: I time the bends and count them heard. How far they travelled, you judge.

cues.say: Start the bend as you pick; reach the top fast.
Pick each bend firmly, once per beat.
Pick each bend once, then let it ring.
Pick each bend right on its beat.
Wait for the beat before each bend.
Count through the rest, then bend on '1'.
Have the next string's finger ready to bend.
Hold the last bend up for its two beats.

notes: A bend is one attack. The app can time it; it does not measure how far it travelled.

selfCheck: Did each bend reach its note, on your ear?

exercises.title: Bend, release, and pick it again
exercises.purpose: The unison bend: bend D on the G string up to the E you're holding on the B string, let it back down, and pick the D you released to. The released D and the notes after it are written, so they're checked.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80.

Ring finger on fret 7 of the G string, first finger on fret 5 of the B string. Pick both, bend the G string until the two E's stop beating against each other, then let it down as you pick D again, then C, and A on the D string.
Bar 1 ends on G and A; bar 2 ends on a long A.
exercises.coachLine: The bend is two strings at once, which I don't pitch-check; the single notes after it I do. The bend's pitch is your ear's call.

Release the bend all the way down to D.
Pick the D again as you release the bend.

Put each beat's long note right on the beat.

Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Keep the shuffle going right to the long A.

Hear the target. The bend in bar 4 is the half step, and the others are whole steps. Each fill stays in the box.
exercises.coachLine: I time every note here and count them heard. The bends' pitch is not measured, so this is one to record and listen back to.

Pick every fill note as firmly as the bend.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Pick each bend right on '1'.
Wait for '1' before each bend.
Count the bend's two beats, then the fill.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Make the last bend a half step, on '1'.

steps.title: The blues in E, down at the nut
steps.goal: Play the box, a riff for each chord and two turnarounds in E with open strings, then all twelve bars of the form in E.
steps.why: E is the key where the guitar's lowest string is the home note. Nothing about the form changes: it is the same twelve bars, with E7, A7 and B7 where A7, D7 and E7 were. What changes is the hand. Down at the nut the open strings do the first finger's job, so the box you know becomes open strings and frets 2 and 3. The Step also gives you two more turnarounds. A turnaround is the last two bars of the form, E7 then B7 here, and it is there for one thing: to bring the band and the listener back to bar 1.
howTo: The form: four bars of E7, two of A7, two of E7, then B7, A7, E7, B7.

E minor pentatonic is E, G, A, B, D. In open position every string is played open and then fretted: fret 3 on the two E strings and the B string, fret 2 on the A, D and G strings. Second finger on fret 2, third finger on fret 3.
The blue note of the key is B flat, at fret 1 on the A string. The second turnaround passes through it on the way up to B.
An open string rings until something stops it. Once you have left a string, let the side of the picking hand or a spare finger rest on it, or the low notes run into each other.
steps.payoff: Twelve bars in E that sound like rhythm guitar: a riff under each chord, and a turnaround that brings the form back to the top.

exercises.title: The box at the nut
exercises.purpose: The four-bar box loop from Step 1, over a band in E, where the open strings take the first finger's place. The same order of strings and the same rhythm, in a new home.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Each string is played open, then fretted: second finger on fret 2, third finger on fret 3.

Bar 1 climbs from the open low E to A at fret 2 on the G string. Bar 2 goes over the top two strings and holds the open high E for two beats. Bar 3 comes down to the E on the D string, fret 2, on beat 3, then the open D. Bar 4 ends on the open low E, held.
Say 'E' on each of the three E's as you pass them: the open low E string, fret 2 on the D string, the open high E string.
exercises.coachLine: The line you know from Step 1, moved to the nut. Notes and the shuffle after the take.

cues.say: Say 'E' on each of the three E's.
Second finger on fret two, third on three.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count each held E's two beats, then move on.
Put each open note right where you count it.
Land each new string right on its beat.
Hold the open low E its full two beats.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: One riff, three chords
exercises.purpose: A one-bar riff on each chord's root: the root twice, then the blue third pushed up to the chord's own third, on up the chord, flat seven included, and back down to the third. E7, A7, E7, B7, four bars that loop.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.

Over E7: the open low E twice, G and G# on the same string (frets 3 and 4), B on the A string (fret 2), the open D string, B again, and G#. Over A7 it is the same shape one string higher: the open A twice, C and C# (frets 3 and 4), E on the D string (fret 2), the open G string, E, and C#. Third finger on fret 3, fourth on fret 4, second on fret 2.

The low B has no open string, so the B7 riff stays inside the open B7 chord shape: B twice on the A string (fret 2), the open D string and then D# (fret 1), A on the G string (fret 2), the open B string, A again, and D#. First finger on fret 1, second finger on the A string and third finger on the G string, both at fret 2.
exercises.coachLine: Four bars and three chords, with the chord changing under you. Notes and the shuffle after the take.

cues.say: Start each riff on its chord's root, twice.
Use the open B7 shape for the fourth riff.
Pick both root notes at each riff's start.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Put each open note right where you count it.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Keep the B7 shape down to the riff's end.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Two turnarounds in E
exercises.purpose: The last two bars of the form, two ways. The first steps down the B string against the open high E. The second climbs the low strings. Both arrive on B7 with the same three notes.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, then quarter notes, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Four bars: the first turnaround, then the second.

Bars 1 and 2: D, C#, C and B step down the B string (frets 3, 2, 1 and open), and the open high E answers each one. Then B on the A string (fret 2), a beat of rest, D# on the D string (fret 1), and B again.
Bars 3 and 4: on the low strings, each note twice: the open E, G# (fret 4), the open A, and B flat (A string, fret 1). Then the same ending: B, a rest, D# and B.
Let the high E ring through bar 1. That ringing string is the sound of the first turnaround. The chords are E7 and B7 in turn, so each turnaround is heard doing its job.
exercises.coachLine: Timed and counted. The open E rings over the line on purpose, so right notes are not checked here: the pitch is for your ear.

cues.say: Let the high E ring under the first turnaround.
Pick every note twice in the low climb.
Leave the beat of rest silent.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Put each open note right where you count it.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Count the rest, then D# and B.

exercises.title: Twelve bars in E
exercises.purpose: The whole form at the nut: the riff under each chord for ten bars, then the climbing turnaround in bars 11 and 12.
howTo: Shuffle eighths and quarter notes, twelve bars, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Four bars of the E7 riff, two of the A7 riff, two of the E7 riff, then one bar of the B7 riff and one of the A7 riff.
Bar 11 is the climb on the low strings: E, G#, A and B flat, each twice. Bar 12 is B, a rest, D# and B, and the form comes round again.
Every riff starts on its chord's root, twice. If you lose your place, wait for the bass to play the next root and come back in there.
exercises.coachLine: Twelve bars over the band. Notes and the shuffle after the take.

cues.say: Wait for the bass's root if you get lost.
Play the A7 riff one string higher.
Pick both root notes at each riff's start.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Put each open note right where you count it.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Count the rest, then D# and B.

steps.title: The minor blues
steps.goal: Play the arpeggios of Am7 and Dm7, find the F and the G# that a minor blues needs, and play a written chorus over the minor form.
steps.why: A minor blues has the same twelve bars with minor chords on the first two: Am7 and Dm7, and still E7 for the turn. The good news is that the box fits the first chord perfectly, since Am7 is four of its five notes. The catch is the Dm7: its third is F, and there is no F in the box. Play the box's E over a Dm7 for long and it sounds unsure. One new note, F on the B string, fixes it, and G# over the E7 does the rest.
howTo: Am7 is A, C, E, G: all in box 1. Dm7 is D, F, A, C: F is at fret 6 on the B string, one fret above the box's E, and at fret 8 on the A string. E7 is E, G#, B, D, as before.
Over Dm7, play F where you would have played E. Over Am7, go back to E. It is a one-fret move up on one string, like C to C#. This time the higher note is the minor one.
A minor blues is usually slower and sadder. Leave the long notes long.
steps.payoff: A slow minor chorus where the F arrives with the Dm7 and the G# with the E7.

exercises.title: Am7 and Dm7, one note at a time
exercises.purpose: Each chord as an arpeggio from its root, then a short phrase that ends on one of its notes. Two bars on Am7, two on Dm7.
howTo: Shuffle eighths and half notes, 50 BPM up to a pass at 70.

Bar 1, Am7 up: A and C on the low E (frets 5 and 8), E on the A string (7), G and A on the D string (5 and 7), C on the G string (5), E and G on the B string (5 and 8). Bar 2 comes down from the high A to the A on the D string.

Bar 3, Dm7 up: D and F on the A string (frets 5 and 8), A on the D string (7), C and D on the G string (5 and 7), F on the B string (6), A and C on the top string (5 and 8). Bar 4: F, D, C, D, and F held.
exercises.coachLine: Two arpeggios and two short phrases. Notes and the shuffle after the take.

Start Dm7 on the A string, fret five.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.

Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count the held A's two beats, then go to Dm7.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Hold the last F for its full two beats.

exercises.title: E7, Dm7, Am7, E7
exercises.purpose: The last four bars of the minor form, called the turn here. The turnaround is its last two bars. Every chord has its own note: G# over E7, F over Dm7, A over Am7, and G# again.

Bar 1, over E7: E, D, B, D, and G# held (D string, fret 6). Bar 2, over Dm7: D, F, A, D, and F held. Bar 3, over Am7: E, C, A, C, and A held. Bar 4, over E7: E and G# as quarter notes, then E on the A string held.

Reach fret six on the D string for the G#.

steps.title: The minor blues in D minor
steps.goal: Play the minor blues in a second key: Dm7, Gm7 and A7 with box 1 at the tenth fret, the B flat that Gm7 asks for, the C# that A7 asks for, and a written chorus.
steps.why: In A minor you found three things. The box fits the first chord. The second chord wants a note the box does not have. The last chord, the one that turns the form round, wants another. All three are true again in D minor, with new names: the chords are Dm7, Gm7 and A7, the note the box lacks over Gm7 is B flat, and the note that makes A7 pull back to Dm7 is C#. Nothing here is a new idea. The Step is here so that the lesson belongs to the minor blues, and not to the fifth fret.
howTo: The form is the one you know: four bars of Dm7, two of Gm7, two of Dm7, then A7, Gm7, Dm7 and A7.
D minor pentatonic is D, F, G, A, C. Box 1 has the first finger on fret 10: frets 10 and 13 on the two E strings and the B string, frets 10 and 12 on the A, D and G strings.

Dm7 is D, F, A, C: all in the box. Gm7 is G, B flat, D, F: B flat is at fret 11 on the B string, one fret above the box's A, and at fret 13 on the A string. A7 is A, C#, E, G: C# is at fret 11 on the D string, and E is at fret 9 on the G string, one fret below the box.

Over Gm7, play B flat where you would have played A. Over Dm7, go back to A. For a line over A7 that comes down to E and C#, let the hand sit one fret lower, first finger on fret 9, and bring it back to fret 10 afterwards.
The band is slow. Leave the long notes long.
steps.payoff: A slow minor chorus in a second key, where the B flat arrives with the Gm7 and the C# with the A7.

exercises.title: Dm7 and Gm7 at the tenth fret
exercises.purpose: Each chord as an arpeggio, then one short phrase played twice: with A over Dm7, and with B flat in its place over Gm7. Two bars on each chord.

Bar 1, Dm7: D on the D string (fret 12), F on the G string (fret 10), A and C on the B string (frets 10 and 13), D and F on the top string (frets 10 and 13), then back through D to C. Bar 2: A, G, F, G, and A held (B string, fret 10).

Bar 3, Gm7 up from its root: G and B flat on the A string (frets 10 and 13), D on the D string (fret 12), F and G on the G string (frets 10 and 12), B flat on the B string (fret 11), D and F on the top string (frets 10 and 13). Bar 4 is bar 2 with B flat where A was: B flat, G, F, G, and B flat held (B string, fret 11).
First finger on fret 10, third finger on fret 12, fourth finger on fret 13. The B flat at fret 11 on the B string is the second finger's.
exercises.coachLine: Two arpeggios, and one phrase in two versions. Notes and the shuffle after the take.

Second finger takes B flat at fret eleven.
Pick every short note as firmly as the long.
Pick only the written string for each note.
Put each beat's long note right on the beat.
Wait for the beat before each long note.
Count the held note's two beats, then go on.

exercises.title: A7, Gm7, Dm7, A7
exercises.purpose: The last four bars of the form in D minor, where every chord has its own note: C# over A7, B flat over Gm7, D over Dm7, and the three notes of the A chord to end.

steps.title: Question and answer phrases
steps.goal: Play phrases that ask and phrases that resolve, and build a twelve-bar chorus from them.
steps.why: A phrase that ends on the root sounds finished. A phrase that ends anywhere else sounds like a question. Knowing that gives you the shape of almost every blues vocal ever sung: say it, say it again, then answer it. It's the point where you stop stringing licks together and start saying something.
howTo: A question often ends on G or C, and an answer ends on A. Start both the same way and only change the ending: the listener hears the relationship.
Blues lyric form is A, A, B: the same line twice, then the reply. Use that form on the guitar.
Over D7, the same line sounds different, which is why repeating it doesn't get boring.
steps.payoff: A twelve-bar chorus that has a beginning, a middle and an end, and uses very few notes.

steps.title: Connecting box 1 and box 2
steps.goal: Move between the first two pentatonic boxes through shared notes, without the seam showing.
steps.why: One box keeps you in a cage. The way out isn't to learn all five at once: it's to find one door. Box 2 uses the same five notes, a little higher, and the G string gives you a slide from one box into the other. That's enough to change how your solos sound, because a higher note on the same scale is a whole new emotion in the phrase.
howTo: Box 2 starts at fret 7 or 8: on the G string it is frets 7 and 9, on the B string frets 8 and 10.
The door is a slide on the G string from D at fret 7 up to E at fret 9. Slide with your third finger and you land in position in box 2.
Box 1 and box 2 are the same notes. A on the D string, fret 7, is the same in both, and you've already found it.
steps.payoff: Your lick climbs out of the box, reaches a new high note, and comes home again.

The second door is a slide on the top string from D at fret 10 to E at fret 12, with the third finger. It puts your hand in box 3.
Go slowly through each new box and say the A's as you pass them. A shape with no roots in it is only a pattern.
steps.payoff: One line that climbs from the fifth fret to the twelfth, with no seam.

steps.goal: Play the last pentatonic box, below box 1, join it to box 1 with a slide, and reach box 4 from box 1 along the top string.
steps.why: There are five shapes and you have four. The last one sits below box 1, at frets 2 to 5, and it is easy to place because its top is box 1's bottom: every note it has at fret 5 is a note you already play. It gives a solo somewhere lower to start from. The Step also closes a gap higher up. You can play box 4, but no line of yours has gone into it yet. A slide you already know, made with a different finger, takes you there.
howTo: Box 5 sits at frets 2 to 5: frets 3 and 5 on the two E strings, the A string and the B string, frets 2 and 5 on the D and G strings. First finger on fret 2, second on fret 3, fourth on fret 5.
The A's are at fret 5 on the low E string, fret 2 on the G string and fret 5 on the high E string. The two at fret 5 are the outer A's of box 1.
The door below is a slide on the G string from A at fret 2 up to C at fret 5, with the first finger. It puts your hand in box 1.
The way into box 4 is the slide you know from D to E on the top string, frets 10 to 12. Make it with the first finger, not the third, and the hand arrives in box 4.
steps.payoff: All five boxes, and one line that runs from the second fret to the fifteenth. Know the Neck moves all five boxes to a second key.

steps.title: A three-chorus solo
steps.goal: Play three written choruses that make one solo: a sparse one down low, one that moves up a box and answers itself, and one that peaks high and comes home. Then play three of your own.
steps.why: One chorus is a statement. A solo is often several, and what makes it a solo is that the choruses are not alike: it starts with room to grow, it builds, it reaches a highest point, and it comes back. Everything it needs is already in your hands: the low end of box 1, the door into box 2, a call and its answer, the slide up to the twelfth fret, a bend at the top. This Step puts them in an order. The three choruses are three Exercises, so each can be learned and checked on its own, and the last Exercise runs all thirty-six bars together.
howTo: Chorus 1 stays on the three low strings of box 1 and leaves whole bars empty. Start with less than you think you need.

Chorus 3 starts in box 2, takes the slide on the top string up to the twelfth fret, climbs box 4 to a bend at fret 15, and comes down through box 2 and box 1 to the low A the solo started on.
Learn them one at a time. When you play all three, let the low chorus also be the quiet one and the high chorus the loud one.
steps.payoff: Thirty-six bars that start low, build, peak and come home: a solo with a shape.

steps.title: A three-chorus solo in E
steps.goal: Play three written choruses in E that make one solo: a sparse one at the nut, one in the box at the twelfth fret, and one that climbs from the nut to the twelfth fret and ends high. Then play three of your own.
steps.why: The solo in A started low, built, peaked and came home. This one has the same parts in another key, and it ends at the top. E gives the idea more room than A did, because here the box sits in two places an octave apart: at the nut, where the open strings do the first finger's job, and at the twelfth fret, where the same shape starts again. The first chorus uses the low one, the second the high one, and the third walks from one to the other. Almost everything in it is something you have played: the box at the nut, box 1 at the twelfth fret, a slide up the top string, a bend at the top of the box. The one new thing is the walk up the top string that joins the two.
howTo: The form in E: four bars of E7, two of A7, two of E7, then B7, A7, E7 and B7.

Chorus 2 is in box 1 at the twelfth fret: first finger on fret 12, third finger on fret 14, fourth finger on fret 15. It is the box at the nut, twelve frets higher.
Chorus 3 starts at the nut with the phrase that opened chorus 1, walks up the top string in bars 7 and 8, bends twice in the box at the twelfth fret, and ends on the high E.
At the nut an open string rings until something stops it. Rest the side of the picking hand on a string once you have left it.
Learn the choruses one at a time. When you play all three, let the low chorus also be the quiet one.
steps.payoff: Thirty-six bars in E that start at the nut, quiet and sparse, and end at the top of the neck.

steps.title: Major and minor together
steps.goal: Play the sweet major pentatonic over the A7 chord and go back to the minor one when the D7 arrives, and hear why.
steps.why: The minor pentatonic over a blues is the sound you already have: tough, a little sour. The players people call sweet mix in the major pentatonic over the first chord, because its C# is the third of A7. Then the D7 arrives, C# clashes with it, and C natural, the minor note, is suddenly the right one. Changing one note with the chord is the first step from playing a scale to playing the changes.
howTo: A major pentatonic is A, B, C#, E, F#. At the fifth fret it sits a fret lower than box 1: the first finger moves back to fret 4 on the A, D and G strings.
Over A7, aim for C# (G string, fret 6). Over D7, aim for C (G string, fret 5). One fret apart, and each is a note of its own chord.
The high position at fret 10, with the first finger on A on the B string, is where a lot of the sweetest blues phrases live. Nothing in it needs a stretch.
steps.payoff: A phrase that smiles over the A7 and frowns over the D7, and a high lick at the tenth fret with the sixth in it.

steps.title: Sixths
steps.goal: Play two-note sixths on the G and top strings over A7, D7 and E7, through the whole form and at the end of a lick.
steps.why: The sixth of the last Step was a single note. Here a sixth is a pair: two notes six letters apart, counting both. On the guitar here that means two notes of the chord with a string between them, and it is the sound of a great many blues intros, fills and endings. One small shape gives you A7; move the lower note down a fret and it is D7; move the whole shape up two frets from there and it is E7. That is the whole form in three shapes that sit within three frets of each other, which makes sixths the easiest way to play the changes with more than one note.
howTo: A7: C# on the G string (fret 6) with A on the top string (fret 5). D7: C on the G string (fret 5) with A on the top string (fret 5). E7: D on the G string (fret 7) with B on the top string (fret 7).

The B string between them must not ring. Either pick the G string and pluck the top string with your middle finger, or let the fretting finger on the G string lean on the B string and strum through all three.

steps.title: Guide tones through the changes
steps.goal: Hear and play the thirds and sevenths that make each chord what it is, and move between them by half steps.
steps.why: If you only play two notes per chord, these are the two. The third and the flat seven of a seventh chord such as A7 tell the ear exactly what's happening, and from one chord to the next they barely move: G falls a half step to F#, C# falls to C. Sing the line. If you can sing it, you can play over the changes.
steps.payoff: A single slow line that spells the whole twelve-bar form without any other notes.

steps.title: Slow blues
steps.goal: Play a full written chorus at a slow tempo, where every note you play is on display.
steps.why: At 60 BPM there's nowhere to hide and nothing to run to. Everything in this Path is a tool for this moment: chord tones to land on, bends that arrive, questions and answers, and rests. Slow blues is the hardest thing on the Path, and it isn't because of the notes.
howTo: Feel the triplets under the beat: each beat has three pulses, and the drummer plays them on the hat.
Play less than you think. Let a held note ring through a chord change if it still fits, and hear how it changes.

steps.payoff: Twelve slow bars that sound like a blues player, with the space to prove it.

steps.title: Slow blues in C
steps.goal: Play the slow twelve bars in C at the eighth fret: the chorus you know, a chorus of long bends, and one of your own.
steps.why: You have played one slow blues, in A. The same form in C puts the box at the eighth fret, where the frets are closer together, and gives the three chords new names: C7, F7 and G7. The thirds sit one fret above a note of the box, as before: E over C7 (G string, fret 9) and B over G7 (D string, fret 9).
The app times a bend and does not measure how far it goes. In a new key the ear has to find each target again, so play the note you are bending to before a take.
